Same all-flipper class in the opposite order, testing whether ' av' at position 0 plus ' nothing' in position 1 still leaves every position out of band, or whether the second position inherits context that restores the ceiling.

A third distinct pair of the space-prefixed flippers, testing whether the predicted zero holds for any all-flipper combination rather than only for the ' nothing' pair the hypothesis uses as evidence.
A non-ASCII flipper at position 0 followed by a space-prefixed flipper, testing whether the predicted-inactive class extends to the UTF-8 byte token 'ão' when it carries no leading space.
The same position-0 'ão' flipper paired with the other English flipper, testing whether the predicted zero depends on the specific neighbour token rather than on both tokens being off-band.
Two flippers that are neither ' nothing' nor ' anyone', testing the claim that any 2-token prompt made only of verified flippers reads below 0.25 of the cap.

The rare dotless-i flipper at position 0 paired with an English flipper, testing whether a byte-level non-Latin token really behaves as its solo reading predicts when it is the first token of the prompt.
Pairs the dotless-i flipper with the only word-like flipper, testing whether ' anyone' leaves a lone Turkish token out of band as the hypothesis's flipper list requires.
The last distinct all-flipper pair, completing exhaustive coverage of the five-token predicted-inactive class so the hypothesis cannot be rescued by a favourable choice of flipper pair.

The hypothesis claims one in-band token restores the ceiling (it cites ' nothing at all' at 0.84), so a flipper followed by an ordinary function word should read active; this is the minimal contrast with the hard negatives above.

At four bells of the morning watch the wind came round to the nor'west and freshened until the sea broke white along the whole length of the reef. The mate ordered the topsail reefed and the foresail double-reefed, and we hauled upon the sheets with numb hands while the deck pitched under our boots. By noon the glass had fallen three tenths and the sky to windward wore the colour of wet slate. No sun was to be seen, only a pale disc behind the cloud, and the birds that had followed us since the Azores were gone.

The captain would not go below. He stood by the binnacle with his coat buttoned to the throat and watched the seas come up astern, each one taller than the last, and he said nothing to any of us until the first green water came over the rail and carried away the hen coop and a cask of salt beef. Then he gave the order to heave to under a storm staysail, and we did it, though it took three of us at the wheel and the loss of a finger to the blocks.

Towards evening the wind veered and began to moderate, and the sea, though still high, lost its ugly cross and ran in long grey ranks from the westward. We lashed the wheel and got what rest we could, half a watch at a time, and the cook served out a measure of rum to every man jack of us. The pumps were sounded and found to make no more water than before. In the middle watch the clouds broke and we saw the stars, and the second mate swore the Southern Cross hung lower than he had ever seen it in these latitudes.

The following day we spoke a brig out of Liverpool, bound for the same waters, and her master hailed us that he had lost two men overboard off the Lizard and had no surgeon aboard. Our captain offered what physic we had, but the sea was too rough to send a boat, and we parted company before dusk with the brig standing to the northward under easy sail.
